Treatise

TREE-tis -- shares a root with 'treat' and 'contract,' both from a Latin word meaning to draw or handle. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Treatise is a formal, systematic written work dealing thoroughly with a particular subject.

The philosopher spent a decade writing a dense treatise on the nature of justice.

Worked Example

A scientist spends fifteen years compiling every experiment, chart, and conclusion from her research into one enormous, carefully organized book meant to be studied by other scientists for generations.

That long, thorough, systematically organized written work on a single subject is exactly what a treatise is. Unlike a 'note,' which can be brief and casual, a treatise is lengthy and rigorously structured.

How Treatise Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dissertation

dissertation: a long, formal piece of writing on a particular subject, often academic

thesis

thesis: a long piece of writing on a particular subject, done as part of a degree

monograph

monograph: a detailed, scholarly written study of a single subject

Antonyms

pamphlet

pamphlet: a small, thin booklet giving information on a subject

summary

summary: a brief statement of the main points of something

How Strong Is It? — monograph → treatise → dissertation

monograph vs. treatise

monograph vs. treatise: A monograph is somewhat similar in scope to a treatise -- both are detailed, focused studies of one subject, though monograph is more common in academic publishing specifically.

dissertation vs. treatise

dissertation vs. treatise: Dissertation can feel like an even more demanding undertaking than treatise: a treatise is simply a thorough written work on a subject, while a dissertation is a formal academic requirement, often the culmination of years of original research.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -tract-/-treat-

root — -tract-/-treat-: to draw, drag, handle (Latin (tractare, from trahere))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin tractare meant 'to handle' or 'deal with,' from trahere, 'to draw or drag.' A treatise, at its root, is a thorough handling of a subject -- the writer draws out every detail and lays it in front of the reader, the same root behind extract.

Use the root in a new word: extract

Use the root in a new word: extract: The chemist carefully worked to extract the rare compound from the plant's roots.
